newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Roche first half profit rises 10 pct.
newsitem.headline: Roche first half profit rises 10 pct.

text.p: Swiss pharmaceuticals group Roche Holding on Friday reported higher profits for the first half of 1997, despite substantially higher costs of launching new drugs.

Roche, the second-largest Swiss pharmaceuticals group, said in its half-year report that operating profit rose five percent to 2.06 billion Swiss francs while net profit rose 10 percent, boosted by higher financial income.
The result was largely in line with forecasts, but was met with mixed opinions, just as expectations had been mixed.
Initally, Roche's certificates were lower in pre-bourse trade in Switzerland, but shortly after the Swiss Exchange opened they reversed direction and bounded higher in a generally weaker market.
A great deal of uncertainty surrounds analysts' forecasts for Roche as it is in the midst of launching three new drugs and will be financing the largest acquisition in its history.

The uncertainty has led to a wide range of forecasts and is not expected to evaporate until it is clear how the new drugs will be received by the market and when the acquisition of Corange Ltd -- holding company for Germany's Boehringer Mannheim Group and U.S. based DePuy Inc. -- is completed.
The $11 billion acquisition, the largest in Roche's 100-year history, was announced in May. However, the deal has yet to be approved by authorities.

Roche has warned the acquisition will dilute its earnings in the first year due to the cost of merging the two businesses and because the transaction will be financed by liquid funds, some of which yield high returns.
In its statement, Roche also repeated that it expected another good result for the full year with an increase in group net profit before extraordinary provisions from acquisitions.
"Barring unforeseen events, Roche anticipates a good overall result for 1997, with a further increase in consolidated net income before extraordinary provisions related to acquisitions," Roche said.

In 1996 Roche reported a 15.6 percent rise in its group net profit to 3.899 billion Swiss francs on sales of 15.966 billion and, on average, analysts forecast Roche's 1997 group net profit to rise 7.2 percent to 4.18 billion francs.

Although Roche's operating profit rose in the first half, its operating margin fell to 22 percent from 25 percent on heavy pre-marketing costs, price pressures, patent expiries and accelerated research & development.

But Roche's financial earnings -- from investing a cash pile of some 15 billion francs -- rose 17.8 percent to 926 million, primarily due to gains on the sale of securities and net currency exchange gains due to favourable developments on capital and foreign currency markets.

Roche expects sales growth to continue in the second half of the year as the rapid global launch of new products in the coming months and next year adds momentum to sales from its pharmaceuticals division.
In mid-July Roche announced a 20 percent rise in first half sales to 9.3 billion francs with the pharmaceuticals division, the company's largest, also reporting a 20 percent rise.
Roche is in the process of launching three new drugs, which the company and analysts' look to with great promise.
Posicor, for high blood pressure and angina pectoris, has received approval in the U.S. and Europe. The other two drugs, Xenical and Tasmar, have not yet received final approval.
Xenical is a new drug against obesity and Tasmar is for Parkinson's Disease.
Roche has expanded its global sales force markedly ahead of the broad-based roll-out of new drugs and in the U.S. alone more than 1,000 new positions have been created since 1996.
Roche expects sales in its diagnostics division to to grow "well ahead of the market average" due to strong demand for the new generation of fully-automated analysers and new PCR tests.

PCR, or polymerase chain reaction, is a technology that allows tiny fragments of genetic material, DNA, to be copied millions of times in a brief period. It thus produces samples large enough for doctors to rapidly detect infectious diseases, cancer cells or inherited disorders.
